vocabulary-context-window.title: Vocabulary and context window
vocabulary-context-window.description: Two different limits: the finite list of tokens the model has IDs for, and the number of tokens it can hold in one pass.

steps.heading: A slice of a 50,000-entry vocabulary
steps.caption: Vocabulary — the model only has integer IDs for a fixed list of tokens. Common words like "the" get their own single ID.

steps.heading: "Zyloprofen" is not in the vocabulary
steps.caption: Out-of-vocabulary words — a word with no ID of its own is rebuilt from smaller subword pieces, so nothing is ever truly unknown.

steps.heading: Turn 12 of a support chat
steps.caption: Context window — the separate cap on how many tokens fit in one forward pass. Here the conversation still fits inside 8,000 tokens.

steps.heading: Turn 40 — 10,300 tokens requested into an 8,000-token window
steps.caption: Overflow — by turn 40 the history exceeds the window, so something must go. Nothing is remembered by magic.

steps.heading: After compaction
steps.caption: Truncation or summarisation — the oldest turns are dropped or compressed into a summary. Whatever leaves the window is invisible to the model.

positional-encoding.title: Positional encoding
positional-encoding.description: Why the same word at two different places in a sentence must arrive at attention as two different vectors.

steps.heading: Token embeddings only: "bank" is identical at position 1 and position 4
steps.caption: The problem — attention is a weighted sum, and sums do not care about order. Without position, "the river bank" and "the bank river" produce identical token sets.

steps.heading: Sinusoidal position signals (d = 6)
steps.caption: Positional encoding — a position-dependent signal is generated. Each position gets its own distinctive pattern of sines and cosines.

steps.heading: embedding + PE
steps.caption: Injection — the position signal is added to the token embedding, so the vector entering attention now encodes both "which word" and "where".

steps.heading: Order now changes the result
steps.caption: Consequence — because the inputs differ, attention scores differ, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" no longer collapse to the same computation.

steps.heading: Four ways to say "where"
steps.caption: Scheme choice — absolute, learned, RoPE and ALiBi all inject order, but they differ in how well they extrapolate past the training length.

multi-head-attention.title: Multi-head attention
multi-head-attention.description: Several attention patterns computed in parallel over the same sentence, then concatenated and projected back.

steps.heading: d_model = 384 split across 6 heads
steps.caption: Split — the d_model-wide token vectors are projected into h smaller Q/K/V sets, one per head. Each head gets its own learned projection matrices.

steps.heading: Head 1 attention weights (each row sums to 1)
steps.caption: Head 1 — this head ended up tracking local order: almost every row puts its weight on itself and the token immediately before it.

steps.heading: Head 2 attention weights
steps.caption: Head 2 — a different pattern from the same sentence: determiners lock onto their nouns ("The"→"bank", "the"→"river").

steps.heading: Head 3 attention weights
steps.caption: Head 3 — a content head: nearly every token reaches for "river", the word that decides which sense of "bank" is meant.

steps.heading: Per token: 6 × 64 → concat → Wᴼ → 384
steps.caption: Concatenate and project — each head returns a 64-dim result per token; they are glued back into 384 dims and passed through Wᴼ so the heads can mix.

feed-forward-network.title: Feed-forward network (position-wise MLP)
feed-forward-network.description: After attention has moved information between tokens, each token is transformed on its own — no mixing across positions.

steps.heading: Post-attention vectors (d_model = 6 for legibility)
steps.caption: Input — one contextual vector per token arrives from attention. From here on the tokens are processed separately.

steps.heading: Width profile of one FFN sublayer
steps.caption: Expand — the first linear layer W₁ widens the vector, usually to four times d_model. More dimensions means more room to separate features.

steps.heading: First 6 of 2048 hidden units for the token "bank"
steps.caption: Non-linearity — GELU (or SwiGLU) is applied element-wise. Without it, stacking linear layers would collapse into a single linear layer.

steps.heading: Back to 6 dimensions
steps.caption: Project back — W₂ compresses the wide hidden vector to d_model again so it can be added to the residual stream.

steps.heading: Division of labour inside a transformer block
steps.caption: Position-wise — the same MLP ran on "bank" and on "river" with identical weights and zero interaction. Only attention moves information sideways.

residual-connections.title: Residual connections
residual-connections.description: The skip path that makes a 100-layer stack trainable: output = x + F(x).

steps.heading: x entering the sublayer
steps.caption: Input — a token vector x enters the block. Hold on to it; the whole trick is that it does not get thrown away.

steps.heading: F(x) — the residual update
steps.caption: Sublayer output — attention or the FFN computes F(x). Notice how small it is compared with x: the block learns a nudge, not a rewrite.

steps.heading: y = x + F(x)
steps.caption: Skip connection — x is added back element-wise. The block only has to learn the difference it wants to make, not reproduce its own input.

steps.heading: The residual stream carries x forward past every block
steps.caption: Residual stream — every block reads from and writes to the same running sum, so information from layer 1 can reach layer 40 untouched.

steps.heading: Gradient magnitude reaching each layer during backward pass (illustrative)
steps.caption: Why it matters — without skips the gradient must survive a product of many Jacobians and usually vanishes. With skips it always has a direct route back.

layer-normalization.title: Layer normalization
layer-normalization.description: Normalisation computed across the features of one token — not across the batch. Each token is rescaled using only its own numbers.

steps.heading: One token's activation vector, mid-network
steps.caption: The problem — activations inside a deep stack drift to wildly different magnitudes, which destabilises the next sublayer.

steps.heading: The six features of this single token, and their mean
steps.caption: Statistics across features — mean and variance are computed along this one token's feature dimension: μ = 1.5, σ² = 13.39.

steps.heading: (x − μ) / √(σ² + ε)
steps.caption: Normalise — subtract μ and divide by √(σ² + ε). The token now has zero mean and unit variance across its features.

steps.heading: γ ⊙ normalised + β
steps.caption: Learned scale and shift — γ and β are trained parameters that let the network undo the normalisation where it is unhelpful.

steps.heading: Each row normalised independently, left to right
steps.caption: Not BatchNorm — a second token in the same batch is normalised using its own statistics. Rows are independent; batch size is irrelevant.

encoder-decoder-types.title: Encoder, decoder and encoder–decoder
encoder-decoder-types.description: The families differ by one thing you can actually see: which cells of the attention matrix are allowed.

steps.heading: Encoder self-attention: no mask, all 25 cells live
steps.caption: Encoder-only (BERT-like) — bidirectional attention. Every position may read every other position, including the ones after it.

steps.heading: Decoder self-attention: future positions masked out
steps.caption: Decoder-only (GPT-like) — a causal mask zeroes the upper triangle, so position i can only attend to positions ≤ i.

steps.heading: Row 3 ("by") of the causal matrix
steps.caption: The same rows renormalise — masking happens before softmax, so each row still sums to 1 across the positions it is allowed to use.

steps.heading: Cross-attention: target rows attend to source columns, unmasked
steps.caption: Encoder–decoder (T5-like) — the encoder reads the source bidirectionally, and the decoder cross-attends to it while staying causal over its own output.

steps.heading: Which layout fits the job
steps.caption: Pick by information flow — do you need to understand a fixed input, continue text, or map one sequence to another?

autoregressive-decoding.title: Autoregressive decoding
autoregressive-decoding.description: The conditioning story: each new token is drawn from a distribution that depends on every token already fixed, including the ones the model itself produced.

steps.heading: Step 1 — prefix length 5
steps.caption: Prefix — the prompt is encoded once. Nothing has been generated yet; the model is conditioning on 5 given tokens.

steps.heading: Step 2 — prefix length 6
steps.caption: Append — the sampled token becomes part of the prefix. The model is now conditioning on its own output, not just yours.

steps.heading: Work done per decoding step
steps.caption: KV cache — keys and values for tokens already processed are reused, so each step only computes the new position rather than the whole prefix again.

steps.heading: A bad sample at step 2 rewrites the future
steps.caption: Error cascade — a wrong token is not corrected later. It is conditioned on, so every following distribution is computed from the mistake.

steps.heading: Step 9 — the model emits EOS
steps.caption: Termination — decoding stops when the model samples an end-of-sequence token, or when a length or stop-string limit fires first.

text-generation-loop.title: The text generation loop
text-generation-loop.description: The control flow wrapped around the model: what your runtime does before, between and after each forward pass.

steps.caption: Encode — the prompt text is turned into token IDs. Everything after this point works with integers, not characters.
One iteration — forward pass, sample, append. This trio repeats once per token and is the only part that touches the model.
Streaming — each appended token can be flushed to the client immediately, which is why answers appear word by word.

steps.heading: Why the loop ended
steps.caption: Stop conditions — three independent rules can end the loop, and which one fired changes how you should treat the output.
Detokenize — IDs are joined back into a string. Byte-level tokenizers must buffer, because one character can span several tokens.

why-hallucinations-happen.title: Why hallucinations happen
why-hallucinations-happen.description: The same mechanism that makes the model fluent makes it confident when it should not be: it always returns a distribution, even with no evidence.

steps.heading: User asks a question the model cannot know
steps.caption: The question — a fact that lives in a private document the model has never seen. There is no correct answer inside the weights.

steps.heading: p(next answer | prompt), no evidence supplied
steps.caption: It must still produce a distribution — the forward pass cannot return "nothing". Every candidate continuation gets a probability.

steps.heading: What the user sees
steps.caption: Fluency hides the uncertainty — the sampled answer is rendered in the same confident prose as a well-grounded one. Nothing in the output signals the 34% figure.

steps.heading: Same prompt at temperature 1.4
steps.caption: Amplifiers — high temperature spreads the mass further, and prompts that forbid "I don't know" remove the only honest option.

steps.heading: Same question, with the retrieved contract clause in context
steps.caption: Grounding changes the distribution — put the actual policy text in the context and the correct answer becomes overwhelmingly likely.

tokenization.title: Tokenization (BPE-style teaching demo)
tokenization.description: Text → subword tokens → integer ids. Common pieces stay whole; rare/long words split. Leading spaces often matter.

steps.heading: Input
steps.caption: Raw text — humans see words; the model will see tokens from a fixed vocabulary.

steps.heading: Teaching tokenizer output (approximation)
steps.caption: Subword split — a teaching BPE: common words/phrases may be one token; long/rare forms split. Leading spaces are often part of the token.

steps.heading: Rare / long word
steps.caption: Rare word splits — “antidisestablishment” is not one vocab entry, so it becomes pieces the model knows.

steps.heading: Token → id
steps.caption: IDs — each token maps to an integer index into the embedding table. That integer is what training and inference operate on.

steps.heading: Consequences
steps.caption: Why it matters — billing, context windows, and quirks like “A” vs “ A” being different tokens all come from this step.

embeddings.title: Token embeddings
embeddings.description: Ids become vectors; similar meanings land nearby in a high-d space — shown here as a labeled 2D projection.

steps.heading: Demo rows (d=6, toy values)
steps.caption: Lookup — each token id selects a learned vector from the embedding table (d numbers).

steps.heading: 2D projection (not the real d-space)
steps.caption: Projected space — royalty words cluster; fruit words cluster elsewhere. Label: 2D projection for teaching.

steps.heading: Nearest neighbours to query “monarch”
steps.caption: Query near neighbours — “monarch” lands near king/queen by cosine in the toy geometry.

steps.heading: cos(monarch, ·) on toy 3-d vectors
steps.caption: Cosine on demo vectors — higher means smaller angle (more similar direction).

self-attention.title: Self-attention
self-attention.description: Q·K scores → softmax weights → weighted sum of V. Context chooses what “bank” means.

steps.heading: Sentence
steps.caption: Tokens in — “bank” is ambiguous until other tokens can influence its representation.

steps.heading: Projections (conceptual)
steps.caption: Q, K, V — each token makes a query, key, and value vector (linear projections of its embedding).

steps.heading: Attention weights α for query “bank” (river context)
steps.caption: Scores → weights — dot products of Q_bank with each K, then softmax so weights sum to 1.

steps.heading: Full attention matrix (softmax per row)
steps.caption: Weighted sum of V — output_bank ≈ Σ αⱼ vⱼ. Mass on “river” pulls the representation toward the landscape sense.

steps.heading: α for “bank” in “The bank froze the account”
steps.caption: Different context — swap in money-related words and the weight mass on “river” collapses; “bank” reorients.

next-token-prediction.title: Next-token prediction
next-token-prediction.description: One forward pass → logits over the vocabulary → a probability distribution for the single next token.

steps.heading: Context
steps.caption: Prefix — the model conditions only on tokens already present (plus system/tools if any).

steps.heading: Logits (slice of V)
steps.caption: Logits — a score for every vocab entry (shown: a tiny slice). Higher logit ⇒ preferred before normalisation.

steps.heading: p = softmax(logits)
steps.caption: Softmax — convert logits to probabilities that sum to 1. This is the full predictive distribution for the next token.

steps.heading: Outcome of this step
steps.caption: One decision — sampling or argmax picks a single token. That is next-token prediction; looping it is generation.

temperature-top-k-top-p.title: Temperature, top-k, and top-p
temperature-top-k-top-p.description: Reshape the next-token distribution: temperature scales logits; top-k / top-p truncate before sampling.

steps.heading: T = 1
steps.caption: Base distribution — softmax at T=1 on fixed logits.

steps.heading: T = 0.5 (sharper)
steps.caption: Low temperature — T=0.5 sharpens peaks; high-probability tokens dominate more.

steps.heading: T = 1.5 (flatter)
steps.caption: High temperature — T=1.5 flattens; the tail (“moon”) gains mass.

steps.heading: After top-k=2 on T=1 distribution
steps.caption: Top-k = 2 — keep only the two largest probabilities, zero the rest, renormalise.

steps.heading: After top-p=0.9 on T=1 distribution
steps.caption: Top-p = 0.9 — keep the smallest prefix of sorted tokens whose cumulative probability reaches 0.9, then renormalise.
